set1.io: Objective a — Review the anatomical structure and function of the skin
set1.q: Which glands become active during puberty and secrete pheromones?
opts: Meibomian glands
These are the modified glands of the eyelid margin and are not the pheromone-secreting glands.
Apocrine glands
Correct. Their activation at puberty is what distinguishes them from eccrine glands.
Eccrine glands
Eccrine glands are functional from birth and secrete thermoregulatory sweat.
Sebaceous glands
Sebaceous glands surround hair follicles and secrete sebum.

set1.io: Objective d — Physical examination findings of abnormal conditions of skin, hair and nails
set1.q: Partial thickness skin loss involving the epidermis, dermis or both defines which stage of pressure ulcer?
opts: Stage I
In stage I the skin remains intact.
Stage III
Stage III is full thickness loss with subcutaneous necrosis.
Stage IV
Stage IV extends to muscle and bone.
Stage II
Correct — partial thickness is what distinguishes stage II from the full thickness loss of stage III.

set1.io: Objective d — Physical examination findings of abnormal conditions of skin, hair and nails
set1.q: A lesion with a central red macule and radiating spider-like arms that blanches is called what?
opts: A spider angioma
Correct — the radiating arms and blanching together identify it.
A cherry angioma
A cherry angioma is dome-shaped and bright red to violet or black.
A telangiectasia
A telangiectasia consists of fine irregular vessels without a central macule.
Purpura
Purpura does not blanch.

set1.io: Objective b — Terms describing lesion type (primary morphology), configuration (secondary morphology), texture, distribution and colour
set1.q: What distinguishes a keloid from a hypertrophic scar?
opts: A keloid contains no fibrous tissue
Both represent replacement of destroyed tissue by fibrous tissue.
A keloid resolves spontaneously within a year
Spontaneous resolution is not a feature that distinguishes the two.
A keloid grows beyond the original wound, while a scar does not extend beyond the injured area
Correct — extension past the wound margin is the defining feature.
A keloid is thin and white in appearance, while a hypertrophic scar is thick and pink
Thin and white describes an atrophic scar.

set1.io: Objective b — Terms describing lesion type (primary morphology), configuration (secondary morphology), texture, distribution and colour
set1.q: Which term describes lesions that remain separate from one another?
opts: Reticular
Reticular describes a lacy or networked pattern.
Discrete
Correct — discrete lesions stay distinct rather than merging.
Confluent
Confluent lesions run together.
Grouped
Grouped lesions form a cluster.

set1.io: Objective b — Terms describing lesion type (primary morphology), configuration (secondary morphology), texture, distribution and colour
set1.q: A palpable, elevated solid mass greater than two centimetres is called what?
opts: A nodule
A nodule measures one to two centimetres.
A cyst
A cyst is encapsulated and filled with liquid or semisolid material.
A tumor
Correct — neoplasms are the example given.
A plaque
A plaque is plateau-like, broad relative to its elevation.

set1.io: Objective e — Clinical skills for a complete and focused skin examination
set1.q: Which finding is described by the term rubor?
opts: Erythema, or redness of the skin
Correct — rubor and erythema are used interchangeably for redness.
Yellowing of the skin and sclerae
That is jaundice.
Loss of normal skin colour
That is pallor.
A bluish discoloration of the skin
That is cyanosis.

set1.io: Objective e — Clinical skills for a complete and focused skin examination
set1.q: Which piece of equipment aids inspection when lice are suspected?
opts: A tongue depressor
This has no role in scalp inspection.
A magnifying glass
Correct — nits appear as tiny white ovoid granules adherent to the hair shafts.
A Wood's lamp
This is not the equipment named for inspecting for lice.
A dermatoscope
This instrument is not the one specified.

set1.io: Objective d — Physical examination findings of abnormal conditions of skin, hair and nails
set1.q: The angle between the nail base and the finger measures greater than one hundred and eighty degrees, and the fingertip is rounded and bulbous. What is this finding?
opts: Clubbing
Correct — the increased angle is the measurable feature that confirms it.
Koilonychia
Koilonychia is a spoon-shaped concavity of the nail plate.
Onycholysis
Onycholysis is separation of the nail plate from the bed.
Paronychia
Paronychia is infection of the soft tissue around the nail.

set1.io: Objective b — Terms describing lesion type (primary morphology), configuration (secondary morphology), texture, distribution and colour
set1.q: A palpable, elevated solid mass measuring less than one centimetre is called what?
opts: A papule
Correct — nevi, warts and lichen planus are the examples given.
A macule
A macule is flat rather than elevated.
A nodule
A nodule lies deeper in the dermis and is one to two centimetres.
A vesicle
A vesicle is fluid-filled rather than solid.

set1.io: Objective a — Review the anatomical structure and function of the skin
set1.q: Which gland secretes sweat in order to maintain body temperature?
opts: The apocrine (scent) gland
Apocrine glands become active at puberty and secrete pheromones rather than thermoregulatory sweat.
The sebaceous gland
Sebaceous glands secrete sebum, which keeps hair and skin moist.
The ceruminous gland
Cerumen is produced in the external ear canal and has no thermoregulatory role.
The sudoriferous (eccrine) gland
Correct — thermoregulatory sweating is the eccrine gland's job.

set1.io: Objective d — Physical examination findings of abnormal conditions of skin, hair and nails
set1.q: Which term refers to a tinea infection of the groin?
opts: Tinea corporis
Corporis denotes the body.
Tinea capitis
Capitis denotes the scalp.
Tinea unguium
Unguium denotes the nails.
Tinea cruris
Correct — cruris denotes the groin.

set1.io: Objective d — Physical examination findings of abnormal conditions of skin, hair and nails
set1.q: Which component of the triple response of Lewis is produced by transudation of fluid?
opts: The reflex flare with broadening erythema
The flare results from arteriolar dilatation.
The fading of the lesion after several minutes
Resolution is not one of the three components.
The formation of a linear wheal
Correct — fluid leaving the vessels creates the raised, edematous wheal.
The initial red line
The initial red line results from capillary dilatation.

set1.io: Objective c — Elements of the history that identify skin, hair and nail disorders
set1.q: Which skin symptoms should be asked about when taking the history?
opts: Fever, chills and night sweats
These are systemic symptoms covered in the review of systems rather than skin symptoms.
Erythema, scaling and crusting
These are findings you observe rather than symptoms the patient reports.
Pruritus, pain and paresthesia
Correct — itch, pain and abnormal sensation are the three symptom categories.
Pruritus alone, since it is the commonest skin symptom
Pain and paresthesia are asked about alongside pruritus.

set1.io: Objective e — Clinical skills for a complete and focused skin examination
set1.q: Which features should be inspected in the nail beds?
opts: Capillary refill time, nail bed temperature and the presence of peripheral cyanosis
Neither appears among the features listed for nail inspection.
Length, cleanliness and evidence of biting
These are not the inspection features described.
Shape, size, colour, brittleness, hemorrhages, lines and grooves, clubbing and pitting
Correct — eight features, each of which can point toward a systemic diagnosis.
Shape and colour only, since the remainder require specialist assessment
The list is considerably broader than those two.

set1.io: Objective e — Clinical skills for a complete and focused skin examination
set1.q: Which characteristics of the skin are assessed by inspection, palpation or both?
opts: Colour, moisture, temperature, texture, mobility and turgor, and lesions
Correct — six characteristics, of which colour and lesions begin with inspection and the remainder require touch.
Colour and lesions only, since the skin examination is essentially visual
Moisture, temperature, texture, mobility and turgor all require palpation.
Temperature and turgor only, since colour varies too much between patients
Colour is a core part of the assessment.
Thickness, elasticity and capillary refill time
These are not the characteristics listed for the skin examination.

set1.io: Objective d — Physical examination findings of abnormal conditions of skin, hair and nails
set1.q: A soft tissue infection around the cuticle or nail fold that is painful and purulent is called what?
opts: Onycholysis
Onycholysis is painless separation of the nail plate.
Subungual hematoma
This is hemorrhage beneath the nail rather than an infection.
Nail pitting
Nail pitting is a dystrophy of the nail plate.
Acute paronychia
Correct — pain and purulence distinguish the acute form from the chronic one.

set1.io: Objective c — Elements of the history that identify skin, hair and nail disorders
set1.q: Which historical factors should be explored for their relationship to the appearance of skin lesions?
opts: The patient's blood type and immunisation record
Neither is part of this line of questioning.
Season, travel, heat or cold, previous reactions, drugs and menses
Correct — each can be the trigger that explains the timing of an eruption.
Season and travel only, since the remainder are rarely relevant
The list is considerably broader than those two.
The patient's height, weight and body mass index
These are not among the relationships explored in a skin history.

set1.io: Objective d — Physical examination findings of abnormal conditions of skin, hair and nails
set1.q: What distinguishes terminal hair from vellus hair?
opts: Terminal hair is pigmented while vellus hair is always white
Pigmentation is not what separates the two types.
Terminal hair is coarse and grows on the scalp and in the pubic, axillary and beard areas, while vellus hair is short and fine and covers the body
Correct — the two hair types differ in calibre as well as location.
Terminal hair is the short, fine hair that covers the body, while vellus hair is the coarse hair of the scalp, axillae and beard
The descriptions are reversed.
Terminal hair grows only after puberty while vellus hair is present only in infancy
Both are present throughout life in their respective distributions.

set1.io: Objective d — Physical examination findings of abnormal conditions of skin, hair and nails
set1.q: Where are the lesions of Kaposi's sarcoma typically distributed?
opts: Confined to the sun-exposed areas of the face and neck
That is the distribution of basal and squamous cell carcinoma.
Confined to a single dermatome
Dermatomal distribution is characteristic of herpes zoster.
Confined to the skin creases and folds
That is an intertriginous distribution.
Widely disseminated on the legs, trunk, arms, neck and head
Correct — the wide dissemination is part of what makes the diagnosis recognisable.

set1.io: Objective e — Clinical skills for a complete and focused skin examination
set1.q: A purple lesion does not fade when a glass slide is pressed against it. What does this indicate?
opts: Hemorrhage in the skin
Correct — blood outside the vessels cannot be displaced by pressure, which is why petechiae and purpura do not blanch.
Vascular engorgement
Engorged vessels empty under pressure and the colour fades.
An allergic reaction
Diascopy distinguishes hemorrhage from engorgement rather than identifying allergy.
Inadequate peripheral circulation
Cyanosis from poor circulation is not what the manoeuvre assesses.

set1.io: Objective d — Physical examination findings of abnormal conditions of skin, hair and nails
set1.q: Beyond the original four melanoma warning signs, which additional letters are included?
opts: E for evolving or elevation, F for family history, and G for growing
Correct — the list extends past ABCD to capture change over time and inherited risk.
E for erythema, F for friability, and G for a granular surface
Neither term appears among the additional warning signs.
E for elevation only, with no further letters
Family history and growth are also included.
F for firmness and G for granularity
Neither describes the additional warning signs.

set1.io: Objective b — Terms describing lesion type (primary morphology), configuration (secondary morphology), texture, distribution and colour
set1.q: An eruption confined to a single dermatome should suggest which diagnosis?
opts: Herpes zoster
Correct — dermatomal distribution is the defining feature of zoster.
Psoriasis
Psoriasis follows an extensor distribution rather than a dermatomal one.
Intertrigo
Intertrigo occupies skin folds.
Tinea capitis
Tinea capitis is regional, confined to the scalp.

set1.io: Objective b — Terms describing lesion type (primary morphology), configuration (secondary morphology), texture, distribution and colour
set1.q: Warts are caused by which organism?
opts: Staphylococcus aureus
This organism causes pustular infections such as impetigo and paronychia.
Human papillomavirus
Correct — verrucae are small harmless tumors of the skin, grey to flesh coloured, sometimes with rough hornlike projections.
Herpes simplex virus
Herpes simplex produces grouped vesicles rather than warts.
A dermatophyte fungus
Dermatophytes cause the tinea infections.

set1.io: Objective e — Clinical skills for a complete and focused skin examination
set1.q: Why should the patient wear a gown for the skin examination?
opts: It prevents contamination of the patient's clothing and keeps the examination table clean between successive patients
Protecting clothing is not the reason a gown is used.
It standardises the appearance of the skin under artificial light
The gown has no effect on how light renders skin tone.
It is required whenever gloves are worn during an examination
Gown use is not tied to glove use.
It allows inspection of the hair, the anterior and posterior body surfaces, the palms and soles, the nails and the interdigital spaces
Correct — a complete skin examination means the whole skin surface, including areas patients rarely expose.

set1.io: Objective b — Terms describing lesion type (primary morphology), configuration (secondary morphology), texture, distribution and colour
set1.q: Which term describes lesions clustered in a dermatomal distribution?
opts: Iris
Iris describes a target or bull's eye shape.
Zosteriform
Correct — named for the pattern seen in herpes zoster.
Herpetiform
Herpetiform describes grouping like herpes simplex rather than a dermatomal band.
Serpiginous
Serpiginous means snake-like.

set1.io: Objective b — Terms describing lesion type (primary morphology), configuration (secondary morphology), texture, distribution and colour
set1.q: Which processes can convert a primary lesion into a secondary one?
opts: Only the passage of time, independent of any external factor
Specific processes are named rather than time alone.
Only secondary bacterial infection of the original lesion
Infection is not among the three processes listed.
Disease progression, treatment, and manipulation such as picking or scratching
Correct — the patient's own handling of a lesion is as capable of changing it as the disease itself.
Disease progression alone, since treatment does not alter lesion morphology
Treatment is explicitly listed as one of the causes.

set1.io: Objective d — Physical examination findings of abnormal conditions of skin, hair and nails
set1.q: A nail whose proximal portion is white and whose distal portion is dark is described as what?
opts: Beau's lines
Beau's lines are transverse depressions rather than a colour change.
Splinter hemorrhages
These are linear hemorrhages of the distal capillary loop.
Terry's nails
Correct — the proximal white and distal dark pattern defines the finding.
Mee's lines
Mee's lines are transverse lines across the nail.

set1.io: Objective b — Terms describing lesion type (primary morphology), configuration (secondary morphology), texture, distribution and colour
set1.q: A generalised or diffuse distribution most commonly suggests which category of disease?
opts: A pressure injury
Pressure injuries occur where pressure is applied rather than diffusely.
An allergic reaction
Correct — a process delivered through the bloodstream reaches the whole skin surface.
A fungal infection
Tinea infections are regional, confined to a specific body area.
A malignancy
Skin cancers follow a sun-exposed distribution.

set1.io: Objective b — Terms describing lesion type (primary morphology), configuration (secondary morphology), texture, distribution and colour
set1.q: What distinguishes a nodule from a papule?
opts: A nodule is filled with fluid, whereas a papule is a solid elevation
Both are solid lesions.
A nodule is flat while a papule is elevated
Both are elevated.
A nodule is transient while a papule persists
Transience is the defining feature of a wheal, not a nodule.
A nodule is deeper in the dermis and measures one to two centimetres
Correct — depth as well as size separates the two, and the examples given are basal cell carcinoma and neurofibromatosis.

set2.io: Objective a — Review the anatomical structure and function of the skin
set2.q: Which of the following is a function of the skin?
opts: Production of clotting factors
Clotting factors are synthesised by the liver, not the skin.
Storage of calcium for release into the blood
Bone, not skin, serves as the body's calcium reservoir.
Filtration of nitrogenous waste from the blood
That is renal work; the skin's excretory role is limited to what leaves in sweat.
Production of vitamin D
Correct. The skin also protects internal structures, prevents entry of microorganisms, regulates temperature and participates in excretion.

set2.io: Objective b — Terms describing lesion type (primary morphology), configuration (secondary morphology), texture, distribution and colour
set2.q: What does the term confluent mean when applied to skin lesions?
opts: The lesions form a line or stripe
That is linear.
The lesions run together
Correct — the opposite of discrete, where lesions remain separate.
The lesions remain separate from one another
That is discrete.
The lesions form a cluster
That is grouped.

set2.io: Objective d — Physical examination findings of abnormal conditions of skin, hair and nails
set2.q: A patient has intact skin over the sacrum with an area of erythema that fails to blanch with pressure. What stage of pressure ulcer is this?
opts: Stage I
Correct — the skin is still intact, and the non-blanching erythema is the key finding.
Stage II
Stage II involves partial thickness skin loss.
Stage III
Stage III involves full thickness skin loss with necrosis of subcutaneous tissue.
Stage IV
Stage IV involves destruction of tissue, muscle and bone.

set2.io: Objective c — Elements of the history that identify skin, hair and nail disorders
set2.q: Generalised itching with no obvious skin lesion should prompt consideration of which causes?
opts: Anxiety and stress, once organic causes have been excluded
The listed causes are organic rather than psychological.
Dry skin, ageing, pregnancy, uraemia, jaundice, lymphomas, leukaemias, drug reaction and lice
Correct — the list spans dermatological, systemic, malignant and infestational causes.
Dry skin and ageing only, since these account for nearly all cases
The differential is considerably broader and includes systemic disease.
Contact dermatitis, scabies and other infestations, to the exclusion of systemic disease
Neither is on the list given for generalised itching without obvious cause.

set2.io: Objective c — Elements of the history that identify skin, hair and nail disorders
set2.q: How should psychological stress be regarded in a patient with a skin disorder?
opts: It should be raised only after organic causes have been excluded
Psychosocial factors are part of the routine history rather than a diagnosis of exclusion.
It is seldom the sole cause, but it can exacerbate many dermatoses
Correct — the distinction between causing and worsening is the point being made.
It is the single commonest cause of chronic skin disease
Stress is explicitly described as seldom being the sole cause.
It has no demonstrable effect on the course of skin disease
It can exacerbate many dermatoses, so it is not irrelevant.

set2.io: Objective b — Terms describing lesion type (primary morphology), configuration (secondary morphology), texture, distribution and colour
set2.q: Lesions confined to sun-exposed skin should raise concern for which condition?
opts: Intertrigo
Intertrigo occurs in skin folds, which are shielded from the sun.
Herpes zoster
Zoster follows a dermatome regardless of sun exposure.
Psoriasis
Psoriasis favours extensor surfaces rather than sun-exposed skin specifically.
Skin cancers
Correct — cumulative ultraviolet exposure explains why these arise where the sun reaches.

set2.io: Objective e — Clinical skills for a complete and focused skin examination
set2.q: Which part of the hand should be used to assess skin temperature?
opts: The palmar aspect
The palm is used for texture and vibration rather than temperature.
The fingertips
Fingertips are best for fine tactile discrimination, not temperature.
The ulnar border
The ulnar border is used to assess vibration in some examinations, not temperature.
The dorsal aspect
Correct — the back of the hand is more sensitive to temperature than the palm.

set2.io: Objective b — Terms describing lesion type (primary morphology), configuration (secondary morphology), texture, distribution and colour
set2.q: A bulla ruptures and leaves a moist area that does not bleed. How should this be described?
opts: A fissure
A fissure is a linear crack rather than a broad denuded area.
An excoriation
An excoriation is an abrasion or scratch mark.
An erosion
Correct — the moist, non-bleeding surface indicates the dermis has not been breached.
An ulcer
An ulcer extends into the dermis and may bleed and scar.

set2.io: Objective b — Terms describing lesion type (primary morphology), configuration (secondary morphology), texture, distribution and colour
set2.q: What distinguishes a primary skin lesion from a secondary one?
opts: A primary lesion is larger than one centimetre in diameter, while a secondary lesion is anything smaller than that
Size distinguishes several individual lesions from one another but not the two categories.
A primary lesion is flat and a secondary lesion is elevated
Both categories contain flat and elevated lesions.
A primary lesion is the one the patient noticed first
The distinction is about the disease process, not about what the patient happened to notice.
A primary lesion forms first and results directly from the disease, while a secondary lesion is a change in that lesion over time
Correct. Identifying the primary lesion is the key to interpreting and describing the eruption.

set2.io: Objective e — Clinical skills for a complete and focused skin examination
set2.q: Why is natural light preferred for inspecting the skin?
opts: Artificial light may distort skin tone
Correct — the distortion can conceal jaundice, pallor and subtle erythema.
Natural light is brighter than any artificial source available in clinic
Brightness is not the reason; fidelity of colour is.
Artificial light makes lesion borders appear larger than they are
The concern is colour rendition rather than apparent size.
Natural light reduces the glare produced by moist lesions
Glare is not the stated problem with artificial light.

set2.io: Objective e — Clinical skills for a complete and focused skin examination
set2.q: Which descriptive terms are used for skin moisture?
opts: Roughness and smoothness
Those describe texture rather than moisture.
Warmth and coolness
Those describe temperature.
Mobility and turgor
Those are assessed by lifting a fold of skin and are separate from moisture.
Dryness, sweating and oiliness
Correct — these three cover the moisture characteristic.

set2.io: Objective b — Terms describing lesion type (primary morphology), configuration (secondary morphology), texture, distribution and colour
set2.q: A linear crack in the skin, as seen in athlete's foot, is called what?
opts: An excoriation
An excoriation is a scratch mark and may be linear or rounded.
A scale
A scale is a thin flake of exfoliated epidermis.
A fissure
Correct — the interdigital spaces of the foot are the classic site.
An erosion
An erosion is a broader loss of superficial epidermis.

set2.io: Objective b — Terms describing lesion type (primary morphology), configuration (secondary morphology), texture, distribution and colour
set2.q: Which term describes lesions involving the skin creases and folds?
opts: Palmar-plantar
That refers to the palms and soles.
Intertriginous
Correct — the axillae, groin and inframammary folds are the classic intertriginous sites.
Extensor
Extensor distribution involves the outer surfaces of joints, as in psoriasis.
Photodistributed
That describes lesions confined to sun-exposed skin.

set2.io: Objective d — Physical examination findings of abnormal conditions of skin, hair and nails
set2.q: Which finding defines a stage IV pressure ulcer?
opts: Non-blanching erythema over intact skin
That is stage I.
Full thickness skin loss with destruction of tissue, muscle and bone
Correct — involvement of muscle and bone is what separates stage IV from stage III.
Full thickness skin loss reaching but not penetrating muscle
That is stage III.
Partial thickness loss of the epidermis and dermis
That is stage II.

set2.io: Objective d — Physical examination findings of abnormal conditions of skin, hair and nails
set2.q: Dry scaling or macerated fissuring of the interdigital spaces of the feet describes which infection?
opts: Tinea unguium
Unguium affects the nails.
Tinea corporis
Corporis produces round plaques with central clearing on the body.
Tinea pedis
Correct — the web spaces are the characteristic site.
Tinea cruris
Cruris affects the groin.

set2.io: Objective e — Clinical skills for a complete and focused skin examination
set2.q: A patient has bluish discoloration of the fingers and toes with a normal oxygen level. What does peripheral cyanosis usually reflect?
opts: Inadequate circulation
Correct — peripheral cyanosis is a perfusion problem, which is why it spares the central mucous membranes.
Inadequate oxygenation in the lungs
That produces central cyanosis.
Excess melanin production in the extremities
Increased pigmentation is a separate finding entirely.
Chronic exposure to cold water
Environmental cold is not the explanation given for peripheral cyanosis.

set2.io: Objective b — Terms describing lesion type (primary morphology), configuration (secondary morphology), texture, distribution and colour
set2.q: How is an atrophic scar described?
opts: Raised and extending beyond the wound
That describes a keloid.
Rough with accentuated skin lines
That describes lichenification.
Thin and white
Correct — as opposed to a hypertrophic scar, which is thick and pink.
Thick and pink
That describes a hypertrophic scar.

set2.io: Objective d — Physical examination findings of abnormal conditions of skin, hair and nails
set2.q: Firm stroking of a patient's skin produces a red line, a broadening flare, and then a linear wheal. What is this called?
opts: Nikolsky's sign
This is a different manoeuvre and is not what the deck describes.
The Auspitz sign
This is a separate dermatological sign not covered here.
The triple response of Lewis
Correct — capillary dilatation, arteriolar dilatation and then transudation of fluid, in that sequence.
The diascopy response
Diascopy involves pressing glass against the skin rather than stroking it.

set2.io: Objective d — Physical examination findings of abnormal conditions of skin, hair and nails
set2.q: A reddish-purple, non-blanching macule measuring two millimetres is called what?
opts: A petechia
Correct — petechiae are under three millimetres.
Purpura
Purpura measures three millimetres to one centimetre.
An ecchymosis
An ecchymosis is larger than one centimetre.
A cherry angioma
A cherry angioma is a dome-shaped lesion that may blanch.

set2.io: Objective b — Terms describing lesion type (primary morphology), configuration (secondary morphology), texture, distribution and colour
set2.q: An elevated, irregular-shaped area of cutaneous edema that is solid, transient and of variable diameter is called what?
opts: A plaque
A plaque is firm, flat-topped and persistent rather than transient.
A bulla
A bulla is fluid-filled rather than solid.
A nodule
A nodule is firm, circumscribed and persistent.
A wheal
Correct — an allergic reaction is the example given, and transience is the distinguishing feature.

set2.io: Objective b — Terms describing lesion type (primary morphology), configuration (secondary morphology), texture, distribution and colour
set2.q: A palpable, elevated, plateau-like solid mass larger than one centimetre that occupies a large area compared with its elevation is called what?
opts: A tumor
A tumor is a solid mass greater than two centimetres.
A patch
A patch is flat rather than elevated.
A plaque
Correct — psoriasis is the example, and a plaque may be coalesced papules.
A nodule
A nodule is round or ellipsoid and sits deeper in the dermis rather than being plateau-like.

set2.io: Objective d — Physical examination findings of abnormal conditions of skin, hair and nails
set2.q: What distinguishes a splinter hemorrhage from a subungual hematoma?
opts: A splinter hemorrhage affects all nails while a subungual hematoma affects one
Number of nails involved is not the distinguishing feature.
A splinter hemorrhage is a transverse line while a subungual hematoma is longitudinal
Orientation is not what separates the two.
A splinter hemorrhage arises from the distal capillary loop, while a subungual hematoma is hemorrhage into the nail plate
Correct — the source of the bleeding is what separates the two findings.
A splinter hemorrhage is painful to the touch, whereas a subungual hematoma causes the patient no discomfort
Pain is not what distinguishes them.

set2.io: Objective d — Physical examination findings of abnormal conditions of skin, hair and nails
set2.q: Hair loss caused by an urge to pull out one's own hair is called what?
opts: Alopecia areata
Alopecia areata is an inflammatory disease of hair follicles associated with autoimmune disorders.
Androgenic alopecia
Androgenic alopecia is male pattern baldness.
Hirsutism
Hirsutism is increased hair growth rather than hair loss.
Trichotillomania
Correct — patches may be single or multiple and range from a few square centimetres to the entire scalp.

set2.io: Objective d — Physical examination findings of abnormal conditions of skin, hair and nails
set2.q: A red scaling, crusting nodule on sun-exposed skin that can ulcerate and bleed is characteristic of which malignancy?
opts: Squamous cell carcinoma
Correct — the face and other sun-exposed areas are the common sites.
Basal cell carcinoma
Basal cell carcinoma is translucent and pearly with raised borders rather than red and scaling.
Malignant melanoma
Melanoma is pigmented with irregular colour and notched borders.
Kaposi's sarcoma
Kaposi's sarcoma produces dark blue-purple macules, papules, nodules and plaques.

set2.io: Objective b — Terms describing lesion type (primary morphology), configuration (secondary morphology), texture, distribution and colour
set2.q: Which term describes grouped papules or vesicles arranged as they are in a herpes simplex infection?
opts: Confluent
Confluent lesions run together into a single area.
Herpetiform
Correct — the configuration is named for the infection it resembles.
Zosteriform
Zosteriform lesions are clustered in a dermatomal distribution.
Annular
Annular means ring-shaped.

set2.io: Objective d — Physical examination findings of abnormal conditions of skin, hair and nails
set2.q: What does the term hirsutism describe?
opts: Excessive fine hair covering the whole body in infancy
That is not the definition given.
Increased hair growth in women following a male pattern of distribution
Correct — the pattern of distribution, not simply the amount, defines the term.
Diffuse thinning of the scalp hair in women following the menopause
That is a form of alopecia rather than hirsutism.
Loss of hair in multiple round patches
That describes alopecia areata.

set2.io: Objective c — Elements of the history that identify skin, hair and nail disorders
set2.q: Which set of questions forms the core of a proper dermatological history?
opts: Where the problem first appeared, what it looked like, how it has progressed, associated symptoms, and what treatment has been tried
Correct. Those five questions cover onset, original appearance, evolution, symptoms and prior therapy.
The patient's age, occupation, marital status and insurance carrier, recorded in full before the skin complaint is discussed
These are demographic details rather than the history of the skin problem itself.
Whether the lesion is a macule, papule, plaque or nodule
Morphology is determined on examination, not asked of the patient.
The results of any previous biopsy, culture and blood work
Prior testing is useful background but is not the core of the history.

set2.io: Objective a — Review the anatomical structure and function of the skin
set2.q: Which gland surrounds the hair follicle and keeps hair and skin moist?
opts: The sebaceous gland
Correct — it secretes sebum directly into the follicle.
The eccrine gland
Eccrine glands open onto the skin surface and secrete sweat for temperature control.
The apocrine gland
Apocrine glands secrete pheromones and switch on at puberty.
The sudoriferous gland
Sudoriferous is another name for the eccrine sweat gland.

set2.io: Objective e — Clinical skills for a complete and focused skin examination
set2.q: How should the scalp be examined?
opts: Ask the patient to wet the hair before inspection
No such preparation is described.
Separate the hair into sections in order to observe the scalp beneath
Correct — the scalp cannot be assessed through intact hair.
Inspect the hair from a distance without touching the patient
The hair has to be parted for the scalp to be seen.
Palpate the scalp through the hair without visual inspection
Inspection is the point of the manoeuvre.

set2.io: Objective e — Clinical skills for a complete and focused skin examination
set2.q: A patient has central cyanosis. What is the usual explanation?
opts: Inadequate oxygenation in the lungs
Correct — central cyanosis points to a pulmonary problem rather than a circulatory one.
Inadequate circulation to the extremities
That produces peripheral cyanosis.
Increased pigmentation of the skin
Pigment change is a separate category of colour abnormality.
Deposition of bilirubin in the skin
That produces jaundice rather than cyanosis.
